name: Sam Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an electric rope shovel at an open-pit coal mine. It's the big digger that loads the haul trucks, and the bucket takes about sixty tonnes a pass. I'm shift lead for the loading crew, so I do the handover, sort out the truck queue with the dispatcher and sign the logbook. It's an older mine run by a small company, so the pay's lower than the big outfits, but it's the only mine within two hours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like getting a truck loaded in four passes, clean, no spillage. Nobody notices when you do it right, but I notice. What wears me out is the twelve-hour shifts and the talk about the mine closing early, which comes round every year. Lena, my partner, works at the pharmacy in town, and between the ute loan and the rent we've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So nothing changes. That's what I'd bet on anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, lots of noise about nothing. At work I'd say the same thing I always say, keep your head down and load the trucks. I don't go online much, so I wouldn't say anything there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI was never my worry, the coal price is. Every year someone in a suit says the pit might close five years early. That's still there whatever happens with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, same shift, same shovel. I'd try to pay the ute off faster, an extra fifty a fortnight. And I'd keep an eye on the news about the coal contracts, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. A bit tight in the chest when the closure talk starts up again, but you get used to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the mine did close early, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know, and I don't like thinking about it. There's a quarry an hour east, but they've got a waiting list. Probably I'd have to follow the work, which Lena wouldn't love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would get cut first if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fishing trips, and the second streaming service. Lena would say my energy drinks. She's probably right.

say: The AI talk was **lots of noise** about nothing.
At work I'd say **keep your head down** and load the trucks.
think: My real worry is the **coal price**, not AI.
Talk of the pit **closing early** is still there whatever computers do.
do: **Keep working** the same shift on the same shovel.
Pay an **extra fifty** a fortnight off the ute loan.
feel: **Tight in the chest** when closure talk starts, but used to it.
S0.quote: AI was never my worry, the coal price is.
fieldNote: His standing pressure is a **coal mine** that may close early.
He avoids thinking about **closure plans**, which fits his dislike of change.
With **two weeks** of savings and a ute loan, he has little room.

steps.text: Keep running the rope shovel on the same shift
Pay an extra fifty dollars a fortnight off the ute loan
Drop the fishing trips and the second streaming service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots spreading slowly. They'll do the trucks before the shovel, I reckon. A shovel's a fiddly thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not the end of the world, there's still work. At work I'd tell the young blokes to learn the truck stuff in case it goes driverless. I'd keep my own opinions mostly to myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my shovel is safe for a good while. Reading a bench and digging it clean is hard to teach a machine. What I'd worry about is my partner. A lot of what my partner Lena does at the pharmacy is checking scripts and answering the same questions, and that's the thinking stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and not rush into anything. We'd cut back a bit in case Lena's hours go. And I'd wait and see what the company actually does, rather than what people say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for me, worried for her. I don't like not being able to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What would make you act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they put a driverless truck in our pit, or if Lena's hours actually got cut. Then I'd start saving properly. Until then it's all talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena if her hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll manage on my pay for a bit and she should look at the hospital. Then I'd go quiet and do sums in the ute. I'm not good at the talking part.

say: It's **not the end** of the world; there's still work.
Young operators should **learn the trucks** in case they go driverless.
think: My **shovel** is safe a good while, because digging a bench clean is hard to teach.
Lena's **pharmacy** checking and answering is the thinking work that goes first.
do: Keep his job and **not rush** into anything.
**Cut back** spending in case Lena's hours go.
**Wait and see** what the company actually does.
feel: **Uneasy** for himself and worried for Lena, frustrated he can't fix it.
S1.quote: A lot of what my partner Lena does at the pharmacy is checking scripts and answering the same questions, and that's the thinking stuff.
fieldNote: He sees his **shovel** as one of the last machines to be automated.
The household risk is **Lena's job**, which is thinking work.
He waits for **hard evidence** before changing anything.

steps.text: Keep running the shovel and not rush into training
Cut the grocery and fuel budget in case Lena's hours drop
Wait until driverless trucks actually arrive in the pit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before the ute's even paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government had better have something ready, because towns like ours can't absorb it. At work I'd say don't panic, there's three years before the robots. I'd keep saying that even if I didn't fully believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think we're in trouble. Lena's job goes in 2028 with the thinking AI, the dispatcher and the planners go too, and once a computer is running the pit, a robot shovel by 2031 isn't a stretch. That's both of us inside five years, in a town with nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything we don't need straight away and put every spare dollar in the bank. I'd sell the ute and buy an old sedan. I don't know what job I'd go for, honestly, and I'm not the type to jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like standing on the edge of a bench that's starting to slump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You told the crew not to panic, but you'd be selling the ute. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I'm shift lead, I'm not going to scare them. But at home I'd be doing what I need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask anyone for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, maybe, he's got a bit put aside. I'd hate it. But I'd rather ask him than have Lena stressed about rent.

say: The **government** must have something ready, because our town can't absorb this.
I'd tell the crew **don't panic**, even if I didn't fully believe it.
think: Lena's job and the **planners** go in 2028, then a robot shovel by 2031.
That's **both of us** out within five years, in a one-mine town.
do: **Cut everything** non-essential and bank every spare dollar.
**Sell the ute** and buy an old sedan.
Ask his **dad** for help with rent if needed.
feel: **Sick**, like standing on a bench that's starting to slump.
S2.quote: Once a computer is running the pit, a robot shovel by 2031 isn't a stretch.
fieldNote: He keeps a **calm face** at work while acting hard at home, and admits the gap.
He sees the **chain**: planners automate first, then the shovel.
He has **no plan** for a new job and leans on family as backup.

steps.text: Sell the ute and buy an old sedan
Bank every spare dollar from each pay
Ask his dad for help with rent if Lena's job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking stuff and 2034 for the shovel. I'd be thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got some time, so the company should be telling us what the plan is. At work I'd keep the crew focused. I wouldn't be making speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably waste the first couple of years waiting to see. That's what I'm like. Then in 2031, when Lena's job goes, I'd be scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe get to a couple of months put away. I'd pay off the ute early. Lena would probably push me to look at a course, and maybe, after a year or two, I'd do a heavy diesel ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not as bad as the fast one, but it nags. Like a noise in the motor you keep meaning to get checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the first years. Knowing that, would you do anything differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to say yes. Maybe I'd let Lena book the course for me so I can't wriggle out. That's probably the only way it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there was no choice. My dad's here, my mates are here. But if it's both of us out of work, we'd go where the work is.

say: We have **some time**, so the company should share its plan.
I'd keep the **crew focused** rather than making speeches.
think: I'd probably **waste** the first couple of years waiting.
Then in **2031**, when Lena's job goes, I'd be scrambling.
do: **Save harder** towards a couple of months put away.
Let Lena book a **heavy diesel** course after a year or two.
feel: **Nagging** worry, like a noise in the motor he keeps meaning to check.
S3.quote: I'd probably waste the first couple of years waiting to see. That's what I'm like.
fieldNote: He is **honest** about his own habit of putting things off.
He hands the **decision** to Lena so he can't wriggle out.
The household still faces **two job losses** within a few years.

steps.text: Save towards two months of expenses
Let Lena book a heavy diesel course for him
Wait a year or two before deciding on training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and then three more for the shovel. The mine might be shut by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a long way off and the coal could run out first. At work I wouldn't change anything. I'd tell the young ones to get a trade while they're at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I've got most of my working years. It's still coal, and coal's on borrowed time, but robots wouldn't be my first worry. Lena's job would have time to change too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save a bit more each year. Maybe in five years I'd look at a diesel ticket. I'm not going to rush it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alright. A bit uneasy about the coal, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had ten years, what would you want to be doing at forty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still working outdoors, ideally with machines. Maybe running a dozer on a farm or a council job. Not sitting in an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change any big plans, like a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might. If the coal holds, we'd try for a small place on the edge of town. With two years' warning, there's no way.

say: It's a **long way off**, and the coal could run out first.
I'd tell the **young ones** to get a trade while they can.
think: I'd get most of my **working years**, though coal is on borrowed time.
Lena's job would have **time to change** too.
do: **Keep working** and save a bit more each year.
Look at a **diesel ticket** in about five years.
Try for a **small house** on the edge of town if the coal holds.
feel: **Alright**, with the usual unease about coal.
S4.quote: If the coal holds, we'd try for a small place on the edge of town. With two years' warning, there's no way.
fieldNote: With ten years, **coal's future** worries him more than robots.
He'd still keep his **thin cushion** and a mine with a closure question.
Longer warning opens up **buying a house**.

steps.text: Keep running the shovel and save a bit more each year
Try for a small house on the edge of town
Look into a heavy diesel ticket in five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Lena's job and mine both going inside five years, in a town with one mine and two weeks in the bank. What would help is the company telling us straight what it plans and when, and some kind of payment while you learn a trade, so you're not choosing between a course and the rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe that people like me aren't against change, we just can't afford to get it wrong. One bad bet and you're done.

headlineQuote: People like me aren't against change, we just can't afford to get it wrong. One bad bet and you're done.
portrait: Sam is a **27-year-old** rope shovel operator and shift lead at an older open-pit coal mine.
He has about **two weeks** of savings, a ute loan, and a partner, Lena, at the pharmacy.
He's **pragmatic**, avoids new tech, and admits he tends to put decisions off.
He thinks his **shovel** is hard to automate but fears Lena's thinking job goes first.
He is **alarmed** in both fast AGI pictures, where both incomes could go within five years.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, with Lena's job and his both gone within five years.
whatWouldHelp: The company being **straight** about its plans and timing.
A **payment while training** so a course doesn't compete with rent.
